awd_titl_txt: Conference: Workshop on Urban Mining and Circular Economy in Construction
awd_abstract_narration:
2516787 (Yin). The Workshop on Urban Mining and Circular Economy in Construction aims to develop a roadmap leading to the advancement and widespread adoption of circular economy in the construction industry. The worshop is scheduled to be held during May 2025 at Washington University, St. Louis, MO. Transitioning to a circular economy is urgent and vital to achieving significant decarbonization, enhancing national economic resilience and fostering national prosperity. This transformation will replace traditional linear construction practices- take, make, consume, and dispose – with a sustainable, closed-loop system that minimizes waste, maximizes resource efficiency, and reintegrates materials into the supply chain. By promoting reuse, remanufacturing, and recycling, the circular approach enables locally available, high-value materials to be reclaimed through urban mining, driving sustainable innovation in the construction sector. Despite its potential, adoption is hindered by challenges such as the lack of advanced technologies, physical infrastructure, and digital systems, alongside entrenched reliance on new materials. Overcoming these barriers requires systemic changes to business models, policies, legislation, and workforce practices to unlock the economic and environmental benefits of building material reuse and recycling.
 
This two-day workshop will convene a multidisciplinary group of stakeholders, including scientists, engineers, construction experts, policymakers, and social scientists, to identify barriers of urban mining and circular construction. Participants will collaboratively develop a roadmap for achieving a sustainable circular economy, while fostering innovation and knowledge-sharing through keynote presentations, panels, poster sessions, and networking opportunities. The workshop will also provide a platform for early-career researchers to share their work and receive feedback. Tangible outcomes include a comprehensive summary of key challenges and actionable near- and long-term solutions.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The U.S. construction and demolition sector is a major consumer of raw materials and generator of waste, creating significant environmental, economic, and supply-chain challenges. As climate impacts intensify and demand grows for resilient infrastructure and affordable housing, the built environment must shift from a linear model of construction and disposal to a more circular approach. Urban mining—the recovery, reuse, and reintegration of materials from existing buildings and infrastructure—offers a practical pathway to this transition. By capturing the value embedded in the nation’s existing building stock, urban mining can reduce embodied carbon, divert materials from landfills, strengthen domestic supply chains, and lower demand for virgin resources. Advancing these practices can help establish a more resilient, resource-efficient, and circular construction economy.

To address these challenges and opportunities, the Urban Mining and Circular Economy in Construction Workshop was convened at Washington University in St. Louis on December 17-18, 2026, with financial support from the National Science Foundation (NSF). The workshop’s primary goal was to develop a comprehensive research roadmap to advance and accelerate the widespread adoption of circularity principles in the construction industry. The workshop assembled a diverse group of researchers, industry leaders, policymakers, community-based organizations, technology experts, and undergraduate and graduate students to evaluate the current state of urban mining and circular construction practices in the United States and internationally.

The specific objectives of the workshop were to:

  • Identify the technological, economic, legislative, and sociological challenges that hinder the transition to urban mining and circular construction.
  • Explore emerging innovations and chat about future directions in urban mining and circular construction.
  • Collaboratively develop a shared roadmap that addresses these challenges and positions the U.S. construction industry to lead in the transition to a circular economy.
  • Facilitate networking opportunities to foster future collaborations and explore potential solutions.
  • Provide a platform for graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and early career investigators to present their work and receive constructive feedback.

The workshop’s discussions focused on advancing strategies that recover, reuse, and recirculate materials from the built environment while strengthening collaboration across research, industry, government, and community sectors. Through keynote presentations, case studies, panel discussions, city best practices, structured roundtable sessions, student research exhibitions, and two plant tours, participants examined four interconnected domains critical to advancing urban mining at scale:

  • Technological advancement and design innovation, including deconstruction methods, material-tracking systems, digital tools, and design-for-disassembly approaches.
  • Economic viability and market ecosystem development, including business models, cost structures, reuse marketplaces, and supply-chain integration.
  • Policy reform and workforce development, including regulatory frameworks, training pathways, and equitable access to emerging circular economy opportunities.
  • Advanced manufacturing in construction and deconstruction, including automation, robotics, and data-driven fabrication processes.

Together, these domains provided a framework for identifying the technical, economic, policy, and workforce conditions needed to accelerate the adoption of urban mining and circular construction practices. Across these domains, participants identified several cross-cutting needs, including improved data infrastructure for material inventories; standardized metrics for life-cycle assessment and embodied-carbon analysis; scalable material-certification pathways; stronger connections between demolition and reuse markets; and coordinated public- and private-sector investment strategies.

The workshop resulted in a research roadmap intended to guide future research, funding initiatives, and cross-sector collaboration. The roadmap identifies priority topics for overcoming the technical, economic, regulatory, and cultural barriers that currently limit the widespread adoption of urban mining practices. By aligning technological innovation, economic systems, workforce development, and policy reform, urban mining can help transform the construction sector into a more resilient, low-carbon, and resource-efficient system. The findings presented in this report are intended to inform researchers, practitioners, funding agencies, and policymakers working to accelerate the transition to a circular built environment. 

The Key Takeaways from the workshop are listed below:

  1. Urban mining represents a major opportunity to reduce embodied carbon and construction waste. Recovering and reusing materials from existing buildings can significantly reduce landfill waste, decrease demand for virgin materials, and lower the environmental impact of construction. 
  2. Technological and data infrastructure gaps remain a major barrier to scale. Improved material tracking systems, digital inventories, and standardized assessment tools are needed to enable efficient recovery, certification, and reuse of materials. 
  3. Economic and market barriers limit widespread adoption. Stronger reuse marketplaces, clearer business models, and improved supply chain integration are necessary to make urban mining financially viable at scale. 
  4. Policy and regulatory frameworks must evolve to support circular construction practices.  Updated codes, procurement standards, and incentives can help enable material reuse and reduce reliance on traditional demolition waste.  
  5. Workforce development and education are essential to implementation. Training programs, academic integration, and workforce pathways are needed to support emerging industries related to deconstruction, material recovery, and circular construction. 
  6. Coordinated research and cross-sector collaboration are necessary to accelerate progress. Advancing urban mining will require collaboration among researchers, industry, government agencies, and community organizations.
